definition: Centralized means gathered under a single point of control — decisions, power, or operations all flowing from one place instead of being spread among many.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word centralized. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know centralized should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After the merger, purchasing became fully centralized: every branch order, from staplers to forklifts, now clears through one desk in Omaha.
Coordinated is weaker than centralized: coordinated branches line up their plans while each still decides for itself, but in a centralized system the deciding itself moves to one controlling point.
Micromanaged goes further than centralized: a centralized office holds the big levers and delegates the rest, while a micromanaged one reaches down to dictate every small step.
To consolidate is to merge scattered pieces into one stronger whole — debts, offices, shipments. Centralized adds a claim about control: the pieces don't just come together, they answer to one point.
Unified means brought into agreement or made one in purpose — a unified team can still share power broadly. A centralized one cannot: centralized says the deciding itself happens in a single place.

Centralized means gathered under a single point of control — decisions, power, or operations all flowing from one place instead of being spread among many.

Under the old railway, every stationmaster kept his own clock and set his own fares; under the new centralized timetable, one office in the capital fixed both, and a train missed in the east could be traced to a minute lost in the west.
Centralized describes an arrangement, not an event: authority, decisions, or operations gathered at a single controlling point.
The railway did not just tidy its schedules — it moved the deciding to one office, which is the word's whole claim.
Its natural opposites are distributed and devolved, where the deciding stays local and no single hub holds the levers.
Centralized is the org-chart word: it describes systems — governments, networks, databases, chains of command — not people.
It also takes sides quietly.
Supporters of a centralized design hear consistency and efficiency; critics hear distance and fragility, since one failure at the hub can stall everything at once.
Keep it apart from plain central, which is merely a fact about position — a central office sits in the middle of town; a centralized office runs everything from there.
The verb centralize names the change; centralized names the resulting arrangement.

Until the 1950s, storm warnings in the region were a patchwork: every coastal town kept its own barometers, its own siren, its own judgment.
Then the forecasting service was centralized.
Every reading from every station now flows to one operations floor in the capital, and only that floor may issue a warning.
Local observers still take the measurements — more of them than ever, in fact.
What moved was not the instruments but the deciding.
A harbormaster who sees the glass falling can telephone, argue, even plead.
He cannot sound the siren himself.
Defenders of the system point to the chaos of 1938, when three towns warned and four did not, and the storm did not care about the difference.
